reasons: All four anchors verified. Vedic side is the textbook collocation: √han- with áhi- as object (RV 1.32.4a, 2.15.1d, 5.31.7b; also 1.32.1c). Germanic: the anchor Beo. 2903 itself has only renewed wyrm and no *gʷʰen- word, so it is context only; the cognate weight is Hym. 22, where OCR 'eiribani' is verified in context as einbani with gen. orms (ON bani < *gʷʰonō, regular). Gen. object + agent noun is a defensible nominalisation of verb + acc. object; serpent noun renewed (ormr/wyrm). Caveat: in Beo. 2825 'bona' is the dragon as slayer of Beowulf, i.e. the relation is inverted, so it is weak support; Völuspá Drepr is not *gʷʰen-. Not generic: bani+serpent in Germanic where the normal kill verbs differ; Vedic and Norse independent.

Verified Il. 17.645 (Ζεῦ voc. + πάτερ opening a petition) and CatAgr 141.2-3. The Latin anchor has Mars + pater (theonym renewed; Iouem only in the preliminary wine offering, not in the address), so the anchor alone gives only *ph₂ter. But CatAgr 134.2 (verified) has the fused voc. Iupiter + precor + uti sis uolens propitius, i.e. *dyeu ph₂ter as a vocative opening a petition, matching Ζεῦ + πάτερ (Il. 1.503, 17.645) and Ved. dyaùṣ pítar (RV 6.51.5a); Umbr. Iupater confirmed in Buck. Both elements cognate, same function, Latin and Greek independent at this level. The Mars pater extension is an Italic spread of the title, not evidence against.

Verified AVŚ 8.6 (āmá- + māṃsá- + ad-, with kravís- in the same verse, of flesh-eating demons), Od. 9.297/347 (κρέας + ἔδω/φαγεῖν of the Cyclops), Il. 22.347 (ὠμός + κρέας + ἔδμεναι, verified), and the Edda prose/verse lines with hrár + eta. Three exact equations: āmá- = ὠμός (*h₂eh₃mó-), kravís- = κρέας (*krewh₂-), ad- = ἔδω (*h₁ed-); ON hrár continues the same *krew-root as adjective. Context congruent: raw-flesh eating as the mark of savagery/monstrosity (also compound ὠμηστής, Il. 24.207, ~ Ved. āma-/kravya- 'eater' compounds). Generic risk is real since all three are basic words, but the triple, fixed in a negative frame, goes beyond chance. Weakest leg: Norse (only 'raw' + 'eat', vikings, not monsters).

Verified Il. 24.528 (δίδωσι + gen. pl. ἑάων), RV 6.23.10d and 9.97.55c (dātár- with renewed genitives), and support Od. 8.325 θεοί + δωτῆρες + ἑάων, Od. 8.335 δῶτορ + ἑάων, Hes. Th. 46/111, RV 8.51.5a dātár- + vásūnām, Y65.12b and VrS27.12a vohunąm + dātārō, Y16.1b. Exact equation in all three: agent noun *deh₃-tor- + gen. pl. of *h₁wesu-, predicated of gods. ἑάων is an otherwise dead archaism in Greek, which excludes chance. The packet's Vedic anchors renew the genitive; the exact Vedic form is in support.

Anchors verified, but none shows the claimed phrase on its passage line: RV 1.157.1b is Dawn shining (the Aśvins only in 1.157.1c), RV 1.92.5d is diváḥ + duhitár- (Dawn, a different title), BV 4989 has Dieva + dēls (singular) in an orphan song (singer climbs to heaven seeking dead parents), not a twin-horsemen context. The real comparison (Ved. diváḥ + nápāt- RV 1.182.1d ~ Gk Διός + κοῦροι ~ Latv. Dieva dēli) has only one cognate element: diváḥ = Διός exact; Latv. Dieva is gen. of *deywós, a derivative, not the same word; the kinship noun differs in every branch, so the second element is free renewal, not a drift of one word. Mythologically strong, phraseologically one element.

The AVP passage line 19.36.26 (vr̥trahan, vīrahan) is irrelevant; the sun clause is in the context line 19.36.25 (sūrya- + gam- + div- acc.). Greek ἀμφιβεβήκει is the perfect βέβηκα, built on *gʷeh₂- (ἔβην), not *gʷem-, so the claimed verb equation fails; 'sky' is renewed (οὐρανός) and the preverb is not cognate. Support AVŚ 6.12.1 is a simile in which the speaker (agamam, 1st sg.) goes around, not the sun. What remains is sun-name + 'go' + sky, which is generic. Unlike C038, there is no *médʰyo- element.

Anchors verified: PlCasin 320 diēs + noctēs as a merism; PlAsina 198 is a list (day, water, sun, moon, night), not a merism; the RV anchor 5.41.7b has no day/night pair at all (only uṣā́sā-náktā in 5.41.7c). The words are cognate (nox = nákt-; diēs and dívā from *dyew- with different formations), but a 'day and night' = always merism is near-universal and both words are inherited almost everywhere, so co-occurrence is expected. Same verdict as C042.

Anchors verified (Hes. Op. 710 ἔπος + ἔρδω, Theognis 307 ἔργον + ἔπος, Aesch. Ag. 1649 ἔρδω + λέγω, Beo. 289 word + weorc; the three Grein lines found by grep in the OCR). Root equations hold: ἔπος/εἶπον and Av. ūxta- < *wekʷ-; ἔργον, OE weorc, Av. varšta- < *werǵ-; Homer has the same pair (Il. 1.504, 15.234, Od. 2.272). But 'word and deed' is among the most common merisms cross-linguistically, the Avestan forms are participles in a triad, not the nouns, and Germanic keeps only one element (word is a renewal). The Crist, Juliana and prayer anchors are Christian and probably calque Latin uerbum + opus, so they are derivative; Beo. 289 is the only native Germanic witness.

reasons: Anchors verified, but all three show only the literal sense: RV 7.55.7d is a sleep charm, Lucr. 3.431 'lulled in sleep', and Beo. 704 swǣfon is the intransitive swefan, not the causative. The cognate causative *swop-éye- (svāpáyati = sōpīre = swebban) is sound. The 'kill' sense is real in Vedic (RV 4.30.21a ásvāpayat with háthaiḥ, 7.19.4d, verified) and OE (Beo. 567 āswefede + sweord, 680 swebban + sweord, verified); Lucr. 3.904 leto + sopitus describes the dead, not killing. So the Vedic-OE match is one cognate verb with the same euphemistic sense; the instrument nouns are not cognate, and 'put to sleep' = kill is a natural metaphor that could arise independently.

Anchors verified. CatAgr 141.2-3 has pastores + pecua + salua + seruassis for the household (pecua = *peḱu; *wiHro- renewed by pastores). The Avestan anchor (gav- + vīra-) and the AVP anchor (gavām aśvānāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ in the context line) renew the cattle word and are weak in themselves. The claim stands on the verified support: Umbr. ueiro + pequo + salua + seritu (Buck, Tab. Ig. VIa) and Av. pasu + vīra (Y9.4e), with YtFra θrāθrāi + pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊ 'for the protection of cattle and men': both elements cognate, the same protective-prayer function, Italic and Iranian independent. The Umbr. seritu = Lat. seruassis match is intra-Italic only. Same grade as C050.

Anchors verified. εὔχομαι and uoueo < *h₁wegʷʰ- is a sound equation. But the only second element is the dative of the god addressed, which is the verb's normal argument and is not cognate (θεός, Mars Siluanus), so this is shared vocabulary, not a collocation. The contexts differ: general piety in Theognis/Aeschylus, a farm vow prescription in Cato. The claim itself concedes it is not a shaped formula.

Verified Il. 8.68 (= 16.777, Od. 4.400) and AVŚ 7.72.3 = RV 10.179.2b (jagā́ma + sū́ra- + ádhvan- + vímadhyam). The hinge, and the difference from C032, is *médʰyo-: μέσον = vímadhyam is exact, and the sun-name is cognate (*sóh₂wl̥/*suh₂r-, different stems). The verb match is at lexeme level only: βέβηκα is built on *gʷeh₂-, jagā́ma on *gʷem-, as the claim itself says. 'Middle' refers to different things (sky vs road), and 'the sun has reached mid-course' = noon is a natural expression, so two cognate content words in the same time-marking role are defensible but not compelling.

Anchors verified (PlAmphi 1123 anguis + uincere; 1119 anguis + enicare). Plautus' Amphitruo adapts a Greek original and the infant-Heracles snake story is Greek myth, so the Latin is derivative, not an independent witness. Lat. anguis (*h₂engʷʰi-) and Ved. áhi- (*h₁ogʷʰi-) are kept as separate lexicon entries and are not an exact equation; the verb is renewed. What remains is the 'hero kills serpent' theme, not wording.

Anchors verified, but the passage lines do not carry the claim. HH Ap. 465 has nothing relevant; the blessing θεοί + ὄλβια + δοῖεν is in context line 466, with goods renewed and δίδωμι. The Vedic anchors use vásu + dhā- (*dʰeh₁-), which is not *deh₃-, so the claimed Vedic-Greek verb equation in the anchors fails. The valid core (δωτήρ + ἑάων = dātár- + vásūnām = dātar- + vohunąm) is real but is exactly C030's support. Taken on its own anchors, 'gods give goods' is a generic blessing.

Anchors verified. Cognates are sound (áśva- = ἵππος; vah- ~ ὀχέομαι/ὄχεα < *weǵʰ-), but the construction differs (horses as subject of active vah- vs a rider conveyed in the middle voice, or 'with horses and chariot'), and *weǵʰ- is the ordinary verb of vehicle transport, so co-occurrence with 'horse' is expected. The claim itself says so.

Neither passage line has the merism: it is in the context lines (AVP 12.18.19 divā + naktaṃ; PlAmphi 168 noctes + dies), verified. Same day/night merism as C033: the words are cognate, but the expression is near-universal and both words are inherited in nearly every branch, so it has no value as evidence. The claim itself rates it low.

Vedic anchors verified and solid internally (dyaús + pitár-, pr̥thivī́ + mātár- as a pair: RV 1.191.6a, 6.51.5a, 1.89.4b, AVP 1.12.5). The Greek anchor HH 30.16 has nothing relevant; the address θεῶν + μήτηρ + Οὐρανοῦ is in line 17. Cross-branch, only *méh₂tēr as title of Earth is cognate: Earth and Sky are renewed in Greek (Γαῖα, Οὐρανός) and *dyéws ph₂tér survives separately as Zeus' title. 'Mother Earth' is typologically very common. Lucretius' pater + aether and mater + terra (1.250-1, 2.992-3) is literary and likely Greek-derived (Euripidean), so it is not independent.

reasons: Anchors verified (FireDed6 ahura- gen. + puθra- of the fire; ása + sonum in Lokasenna 56/64, Grímnismál 43, Hymiskviða 3). ON áss < *ansuz and Ved./Av. ásura-/ahura- belong to one root (*h₂ems-u- vs the -ro- derivative), but they are not the same formation, and the son-word is never cognate where the two co-occur (puθra-/putrá- vs sonr). Vedic support is misread: in RV 10.56.6a ásuram is the accusative object of the verb, not a genitive with sūnávaḥ; in RV 3.53.7b/10.67.2b putrā́saḥ goes with diváḥ, and ásurasya with vīrā́ḥ. Avestan 'son of Ahura Mazdā' is a singular epithet of fire, the Norse a collective name for the gods. 'Sons of the god(s)' is generic. Same grade as C045.

Same phrase as C044. The Vedic anchor RV 10.132.4a has only voc. asura beside dyaús, no 'sons' phrase. The support is misread: in RV 3.53.7b and 10.67.2b putrā́saḥ construes with diváḥ ('sons of Heaven') and ásurasya with vīrā́ḥ ('heroes of the Asura'), so there is no 'sons of the Asura' collocation; in RV 10.10.2c putrā́saḥ goes with maháḥ. The root link *ansuz ~ ásura- is plausible but derivationally distinct, the son-word is not cognate, and the notion is generic.

Anchors verified (RV 7.4.5b amŕ̥ta- for the gods; RV 6.16.32c márta-; Od. 1.66-67 βροτός vs ἀθάνατος + θεός; Cato Orig. dii + immortales). Exact equation Ved. amŕ̥ta- = Gk ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥tó-) as the epithet of gods (RV 10.66.13d devá- + amŕ̥ta-; Il. 24.460 θεός + ἄμβροτος, verified), set against *mr̥tó-/*mórto- 'mortal' used as a noun for humans (márta- ~ βροτός, same root, different ablaut). Two cognate elements in the same gods-vs-mortals polarity. Greek mostly renews the epithet with ἀθάνατος, as in the Od. 1.67 context line. Latin immortalis is a fresh formation and possibly a Greek calque, so acceptance rests on Vedic and Greek. Generic risk is medium, since gods are commonly called 'deathless'.

Anchors verified (Il. 24.417 ἠώς + δῖα + φαίνομαι; Il. 1.477; Od. 13.94 φάος + Ἠώς; RV 3.61.5a devī́- + uṣás- + vi-bhā-; 7.78.3b; 6.65.2b; 4.1.17b uṣás- + bhānú-). Equations hold: *h₂éwsōs exact, Ved. bhā- ~ Gk φαν-/φάος < *bʰeh₂-, though with different stems (root present vs -n-yé-; -nu- vs -wos). The epithets are different derivatives (devī́ vs δῖα). The collocation is formulaic in both corpora, but 'Dawn shines/appears' is what any language with these two inherited words would say, so co-occurrence is largely expected. Defensible, not compelling.

AVŚ 13.1.47 verified: the bay horses of the Sun, amŕ̥ta-, draw his chariot. The Greek anchor HH Cer. 375 lacks the adjective; ἀθάνατος (renewed) is in line 376. The exact equation is in verified support: Il. 16.380-381 ἵπποι + ἄμβροτοι (Achilles' god-given horses). Both elements are exact cognates (*h₁éḱwos = áśva-/ἵππος; *n̥-mr̥tó- = amŕ̥ta-/ἄμβροτος), in attributive agreement, of divine teams. Medium generic risk: 'immortal' is freely applied to divine things in both traditions. The ὄχος/vah- part is incidental.

Anchors verified. The cognates are sound (*h₁ed- in ad-/ἔδω/edo; *peh₃- in píbati/πίνω/bibo, same reduplicated present). But 'eat and drink' as a pair for nourishment is about as generic as phraseology gets, the anchor contexts are heterogeneous (gods, hospitality, Cato's cabbage diet, an epitaph), and the frequent Greek renewals (φαγεῖν, ἐσθίω) show no fixed wording. The claim itself flags the generic risk.

The same *wiHrō- + *peḱu- protective formula as C036, so the same grade. It is true on verified support: Umbr. ueiro + pequo + salua + seritu (Buck) and Av. θrāθrāi + pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊ (YtFra2.10e, 12.4e), with both elements cognate in protective prayer. This claim's own anchors add little: AVŚ 4.21.14 and AVP 19.14.24 have gó- 'cow', not paśu-, and no vīra-; CatAgr 149.2 is a legal clause in a pasture-sale contract, not a prayer; the averting verbs are not cognate; the Mars-Rudra parallel is typological only. RV 1.114.8 (gó-, áśva-, vīrá-) is Vedic-internal.

Anchors verified (AVŚ 4.22.14-15 eka-vr̥ṣa- 'sole bull' of the king; Il. 2.480-482 βοῦς/ταῦρος simile for Agamemnon). Only *gʷṓws is cognate, and it is incidental. The bull words and the superlatives are not cognate, and the king-as-bull image is widespread typology. A shared figure, not shared wording, as the claim itself says.

Anchors verified; the Greek anchor Od. 15.106 is Helen (δῖα + γυναικῶν), not Dawn. The cross-branch link depends on the contested Helen = Dawn/Sun-maiden identification. Ved. devī́ (*deywih₂, simply 'goddess') and Gk δῖα (*diwyeh₂) are different derivatives. Both are default epithets for any goddess or heroine, so 'goddess Dawn' ~ Ἠώς + δῖα (Il. 9.240, verified) is expected by chance. Only *h₂éwsōs is exact. Unlike C047, there is no cognate verb.
